items.title: HTB: PingPong
items.summary: PingPong is an assume breach Active Directory box with two forests joined by a bidirectional trust. I’ll abuse ESC13 to get a certificate whose issuance policy maps to a group with WinRM access, and get a shell on the first DC. From there, I’ll tunnel to the second forest, convert a global group to domain local so I can add my user from across the trust, and read a gMSA password. That gMSA account is limited to a constrained JEA endpoint, which I’ll escape with script blocks to find credentials in a PowerShell history file. With those, I’ll abuse resource-based constrained delegation to reach MSSQL as a database admin, and use GodPotato to compromise the second domain. Finally, I’ll cross back over the trust and abuse ESC4 to get Administrator on the first DC.

items.title: CrowdStrike in Talks to Acquire Zscaler in One of the Biggest Cybersecurity Deals Ever
items.summary: CrowdStrike is in talks to acquire Zscaler in a deal that could rank among the largest in cybersecurity history. Bloomberg first reported the discussions on Friday, November 20, citing two people familiar with the matter who said talks were ongoing. The discussions could still end without an agreement. Neither company has announced a deal or disclosed a proposed purchase price. Zscaler shares jumped 18% in extended trading Friday, while CrowdStrike shares fell more than 8%. CrowdStrike declined to comment, and Zscaler did not immediately respond to CNBC’s request. At Friday’s regular close, Zscaler was worth about $32 billion. That figure reflects the stock market’s valuation, not what CrowdStrike has offered or might ultimately pay. Zscaler Would Add to CrowdStrike Falcon CrowdStrike’s Falcon platform helps security teams detect and stop threats on laptops, servers, and cloud workloads. Zscaler controls how users and devices connect to applications and the internet. Its Zero Trust Exchange checks identity and other signs of risk before allowing access. The two products address different parts of the same problem: Falcon can spot suspicious activity, while Zscaler can limit what a user or device can reach. The companies already work together. A day before the takeover reports, CrowdStrike previewed an integration that lets Falcon share changes in user risk with Zscaler’s Adaptive Access Engine through open standards. For example, if Falcon flags a user as risky after sign-in, Zscaler can use that signal to tighten access without waiting for the user to log in again. That work builds on a partnership expansion announced in September and is separate from the reported acquisition talks. CrowdStrike’s earlier agreement to buy SGNL also focused on changing access as risk changes, rather than letting permissions stand until someone removes them. Buying Zscaler would go further by bringing a cloud service that manages access to private applications and the public internet under the same owner as Falcon. The companies have not announced any plans to combine products or change customer contracts. The talks come as major vendors buy tools that extend their reach beyond their main products. Google closed its $32 billion acquisition of Wiz in March 2026, adding cloud security tools to Google Cloud. Palo Alto Networks completed its $25 billion purchase of CyberArk earlier this year, expanding into tools that protect accounts with powerful system permissions. Both are completed deals. Zscaler’s market value shows why the CrowdStrike talks matter, but it cannot yet be used to rank the proposed purchase. For security teams, the practical question is whether common ownership would make it easier to investigate an alert and restrict access without switching tools. Teams that use only one of the products would also want to know whether existing links to other vendors would remain supported and whether pricing would change. For now, the existing partnership shows how the products can work together. It does not tell customers how a combined company would sell or support them. items.title: 6 Critical F5 BIG-IP Vulnerabilities Could Let Hackers Disrupt Websites and Execute Malicious Code
items.summary: F5 released emergency fixes for six critical BIG-IP vulnerabilities that could let remote attackers take websites and other services offline without logging in. The flaws affect specific traffic-handling configurations. An attacker who can reach a vulnerable service could crash the BIG-IP process that handles client traffic. F5 also warned that attackers may be able to run code on affected devices. The company disclosed the flaws in its November 18 out-of-band security notification . The advisory said no exploitation had been reported at the time. That sets this disclosure apart from the BIG-IP OAuth zero-day reported in September , which F5 said attackers were already exploiting. BIG-IP Flaws Take Websites Offline BIG-IP often sits between users and the servers that host a website. Its Traffic Management Microkernel, or TMM, handles connections passing through the device. If that process crashes, users can lose access even when the web servers behind it are still running. The impact is not limited to websites. Remote access portals and other applications that rely on the same device can also become unavailable. These are data-plane flaws, meaning they affect the part of BIG-IP that handles live traffic rather than the interface administrators use to manage it. Keeping the management interface off the internet does not fix the problem if an affected service is still reachable. The result can look similar to an outage caused by the earlier BIG-IP HTTP/2 denial-of-service flaw , but the new flaws involve memory corruption rather than exhaustion of processing power. BIG-IP Deployments Affected Five of the six flaws affect iRules, the scripts administrators use to control how BIG-IP handles traffic. They are CVE-2026-120285, CVE-2026-120292, CVE-2026-116953, CVE-2026-120722 and CVE-2026-121805. Some also affect BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes or BIG-IP Cloud-Native Network Functions. Teams should check the advisory for each flaw against the product and configuration they actually run. The sixth flaw, CVE-2026-123637 , affects BIG-IP Access Policy Manager when a virtual server uses a per-request policy with both the Client Information and Endpoint Security agents. A separate single sign-on flaw, CVE-2026-126822, can also cause an outage without a login, but it is rated high severity and is not part of the six critical issues. F5’s engineering hotfix guide covers BIG-IP TMOS 17.1.x, 17.5.x and 21.1.x. The correct package depends on the exact base release or engineering build already installed. items.title: WhatsApp Android Flaws Could Let Hackers Delete Users’ Files and Expose IP Addresses
items.summary: WhatsApp’s November 2026 security update describes three flaws that could let attackers delete files stored by WhatsApp on Android, expose a user’s IP address, or bypass a security check for Meta AI’s Private Processing service. Of the three, only the IP exposure flaw was flagged for possible abuse. The advisory says it may have been used alongside specific spam messages, but it does not say how many users may have been affected. WhatsApp Android Flaw Could Delete Local Files CVE-2026-102769 is a SQL injection flaw affecting WhatsApp for Android before version 2.26.35.74. SQL injection occurs when an app treats input as part of a database command rather than as data. According to the November advisory, file deletion required the recipient to tap an “order details” message. The advisory limits the possible damage to files stored locally by WhatsApp, not files across the device. The same flaw could also reveal one bit of information about the recipient’s chat database if they were online when the message arrived. That is a limited leak, not evidence that an attacker could read entire conversations. An external researcher reported the issue through Meta’s security reporting program. WhatsApp said it had seen no evidence of exploitation. CVE-2026-23871 affects WhatsApp and WhatsApp Business for Android before version 2.26.17.4. The app did not fully check external media links in replies tied to Click to WhatsApp ads. A device could reveal its IP address when WhatsApp displayed the message in a chat. Unlike the file deletion flaw, the advisory does not describe a tap as necessary. An IP address is network information, not the contents of a chat. Cyber Security News previously covered a separate WhatsApp flaw involving Instagram Reels that also involved incomplete checks on media links. The two issues carry different CVE IDs and affect different app versions. CVE-2026-44908 affected how WhatsApp verified the identity of servers used by Meta AI’s Private Processing service . The flaw could have let someone positioned inside Meta’s infrastructure bypass a check meant to confirm that the server was running on trusted hardware. The advisory says the certificate would first have had to appear in a third-party record. All published certificates traced back to trusted hardware, which WhatsApp says confirms the flaw was not exploited. The certificate fix arrived in WhatsApp 2.26.24.72 for iOS, 2.26.23.74 for Android, and 2.26.23.72 for Mac. WhatsApp Business received fixes in 2.26.23.72 for iOS and 2.26.23.70 for Android. Users should install the latest available version from their official app store and check WhatsApp Business separately if they use both apps. The WhatsApp Security Advisories page notes that app store release notes may not list every security fix. What Are Leading Organizations Doing About AI and Cyber Risks? Find Out. View Details!

Introduction iTerm2’s Kitty image protocol implementation has a remote code execution vulnerability in the file transmit error response path. An APC escape sequence embedded in any file is consumed by the VT100 parser and does not appear in the cat output itself, but the Kitty file transmit error response preserves literal newlines from a crafted file path and writes them to PTY stdin — the shell interprets these newlines as command separators, resulting in arbitrary command execution. This is a logic bug — no memory corruption or race condition required — and is 100% reproducible. It works on a default iTerm2 installation with no configuration changes, and triggers on all shells including bash, zsh, and fish . Affected Versions Affected Fixed Prerequisite All versions with Kitty Image Protocol support 3.7.9 iTerm2 installed (default settings) Vulnerability Three independent issues combine into a single exploit chain: (1) the APC handler lacks the trust check present in OSC handlers, (2) the Kitty file transmit error path preserves literal newlines from NSError.localizedDescription , and (3) the response is unconditionally written to PTY stdin. APC Processing — No Trust Check When the VT100 parser receives an APC sequence, it calls executeAPC: . At [A], it checks for tmux mode — if active, it returns early. At [B], it checks only whether the string starts with “G”, and at [C] creates a Kitty image command and passes it to the delegate. Compared to OSC sequence handling, the terminalIsTrusted check is completely absent . Any APC that reaches the VT100 parser is unconditionally executed regardless of source. // sources/VT100/VT100Terminal.m — executeAPC: - ( void ) executeAPC :( VT100Token * ) token { if ( _tmuxMode ) { // [A] [ _delegate terminalSetWindowTitle :...]; return ; } if ([ token . string hasPrefix : @"G" ]) { // [B] iTermKittyImageCommand * command = [[ iTermKittyImageCommand alloc ] initWithAPCString: [ token . string substringFromIndex : 1 ]]; if ( ! command ) { return ; } [ _delegate terminalDidReceiveKittyImageCommand : command ]; // [C] } } No trust check exists in the delegate chain either. At [A], the command is passed directly to kittyImageController . // sources/VT100Screen/VT100ScreenMutableState+TerminalDelegate.m - ( void ) terminalDidReceiveKittyImageCommand :( iTermKittyImageCommand * ) command { [ _kittyImageController execute : command ]; // [A] } Kitty File Transmit — Error Newline Preservation When the Kitty image controller receives a t=f (file transmit) command, it decodes the base64 payload and uses it as a file path. At [A], URL.resourceValues() checks whether the file exists — if it doesn’t, an exception is thrown. At [B], the filenameIsSafe() blocklist check exists, but this code is only reachable after resourceValues() succeeds, so it never executes for non-existent files . At [C], the catch block embeds error.localizedDescription directly into the error message. macOS’s NSError.localizedDescription preserves literal newlines (0x0A) in filenames without escaping them. // sources/InlineImages/KittyImageController.swift — handle(command:fileURL:query:) private func handle ( command : KittyImageCommand . ImageTransmission , fileURL : URL , query : Bool ) -> String ? { do { let values = try fileURL . resourceValues ( forKeys : [ . isRegularFileKey ]) // [A] guard values . isRegularFile == true else { return "EBADF:Not a file" } guard filenameIsSafe ( fileURL : fileURL ) else { // [B] return "EBADF:Invalid path" } let content = try Data ( contentsOf : fileURL ) return handle ( command : command , data : content , query : query ) } catch { return "EBADF: \( error . localizedDescription ) " // [C] } } Response Written to PTY Stdin The response containing the error message is written to PTY stdin. At [A], the default verbosity .normal always sends the response — it is sent regardless of whether it is an error. At [B], the response is wrapped in APC format ( ESC_G...ESC\ ) and passed to the delegate. // sources/InlineImages/KittyImageController.swift — respondToTransmit() func respondToTransmit ( _ imageTransmission : KittyImageCommand . Introduction

iTerm2’s Kitty image protocol implementation has a remote code execution vulnerability in the file transmit error response path. An APC escape sequence embedded in any file is consumed by the VT100 parser and does not appear in the cat output itself, but the Kitty file transmit error response preserves literal newlines from a crafted file path and writes them to PTY stdin — the shell interprets these newlines as command separators, resulting in arbitrary command execution.
This is a logic bug — no memory corruption or race condition required — and is 100% reproducible. It works on a default iTerm2 installation with no configuration changes, and triggers on all shells including bash, zsh, and fish.


Affected Versions Affected Fixed Prerequisite All versions with Kitty Image Protocol support 3.7.9 iTerm2 installed (default settings)


Vulnerability

Three independent issues combine into a single exploit chain: (1) the APC handler lacks the trust check present in OSC handlers, (2) the Kitty file transmit error path preserves literal newlines from NSError.localizedDescription, and (3) the response is unconditionally written to PTY stdin.


APC Processing — No Trust Check

When the VT100 parser receives an APC sequence, it calls executeAPC:. At [A], it checks for tmux mode — if active, it returns early. At [B], it checks only whether the string starts with “G”, and at [C] creates a Kitty image command and passes it to the delegate. Compared to OSC sequence handling, the terminalIsTrusted check is completely absent. Any APC that reaches the VT100 parser is unconditionally executed regardless of source.

// sources/VT100/VT100Terminal.m — executeAPC:

- (void)executeAPC:(VT100Token *)token {
    if (_tmuxMode) {                                                // [A]
        [_delegate terminalSetWindowTitle:...];
        return;
    }
    if ([token.string hasPrefix:@"G"]) {                            // [B]
        iTermKittyImageCommand *command =
            [[iTermKittyImageCommand alloc]
                initWithAPCString:[token.string substringFromIndex:1]];
        if (!command) {
            return;
        }
        [_delegate terminalDidReceiveKittyImageCommand:command];    // [C]
    }
}


No trust check exists in the delegate chain either. At [A], the command is passed directly to kittyImageController.

// sources/VT100Screen/VT100ScreenMutableState+TerminalDelegate.m

- (void)terminalDidReceiveKittyImageCommand:(iTermKittyImageCommand *)command {
    [_kittyImageController execute:command];                        // [A]
}


Kitty File Transmit — Error Newline Preservation

When the Kitty image controller receives a t=f (file transmit) command, it decodes the base64 payload and uses it as a file path. At [A], URL.resourceValues() checks whether the file exists — if it doesn’t, an exception is thrown. At [B], the filenameIsSafe() blocklist check exists, but this code is only reachable after resourceValues() succeeds, so it never executes for non-existent files. At [C], the catch block embeds error.localizedDescription directly into the error message. macOS’s NSError.localizedDescription preserves literal newlines (0x0A) in filenames without escaping them.

// sources/InlineImages/KittyImageController.swift — handle(command:fileURL:query:)

private func handle(command: KittyImageCommand.ImageTransmission,
                    fileURL: URL,
                    query: Bool) -> String? {
    do {
        let values = try fileURL.resourceValues(forKeys: [.isRegularFileKey])  // [A]
        guard values.isRegularFile == true else {
            return "EBADF:Not a file"
        }
        guard filenameIsSafe(fileURL: fileURL) else {                           // [B]
            return "EBADF:Invalid path"
        }
        let content = try Data(contentsOf: fileURL)
        return handle(command: command, data: content, query: query)
    } catch {
        return "EBADF:\(error.localizedDescription)"                            // [C]
    }
}


Response Written to PTY Stdin

The response containing the error message is written to PTY stdin. At [A], the default verbosity .normal always sends the response — it is sent regardless of whether it is an error. At [B], the response is wrapped in APC format (ESC_G...ESC\) and passed to the delegate.

// sources/InlineImages/KittyImageController.swift — respondToTransmit()

func respondToTransmit(_ imageTransmission: KittyImageCommand.ImageTransmission,
                        display: KittyImageCommand.ImageDisplay?,
                        error: String?) {
    if imageTransmission.more == .expectMore {
        return
    }
    var args = [String]()
    args.append("i=\(imageTransmission.identifier)")
    // ...
    let payload = args.joined(separator: ",") + semi + (error ?? "OK")
    let message = "\u{1B}_G\(payload)\u{1B}\\"

    switch imageTransmission.verbosity {
    case .normal:                                                               // [A]
        delegate?.kittyImageControllerReport(message: message)                  // [B]
    case .query:
        if error != nil {
            delegate?.kittyImageControllerReport(message: message)
        }
        return
    case .quiet:
        return
    }
}


At the end of the delegate chain, [A] the response data is written to the PTY via screenSendReportData:. This function sends data through the same path as keyboard input, so the shell interprets this data as if the user typed it.

// sources/VT100Screen/VT100ScreenMutableState.m — kittyImageControllerReportWithMessage:

- (void)kittyImageControllerReportWithMessage:(NSString *)string {
    [self willSendReport];
